source: Ilic (2023, rev 2024) Unveiling the General Intelligence Factor in Language Models
finding: Factor analysis of LLM leaderboards finds one dominant factor, much stronger than the g seen in people.
numbers: Open LLM Leaderboard: 1,232 models, 22 subtests; first factor 85.4% of variance (87% with a 2nd factor). GLUE: 88 models, 10 subtests, about 85%. Loadings .57 (TruthfulQA) to .98; mean about .92 (human about .6). KMO .98; RMSR .02. g scores from disjoint batteries r=.99. Kendall tau with model size .49 (CI .46-.53).
limits: Parallel analysis suggested 2 factors; two-factor solution factors correlated .8 to .85. Exploratory only, mean imputation, 88-model GLUE sample is small, battery narrow (mostly MMLU-style multiple choice).
agent_relevance: Benchmark scores of LLMs are very correlated, so one ability number mostly tracks model scale and recipe. Do not read separate benchmark gains as separate skills.

source: Ilic (2023) Open LLM Leaderboard analysis, retention rules
finding: Retention tests disagreed on factor count, which weakens the single-g reading.
numbers: MAP, scree and Kaiser suggested 1 factor; Horn parallel analysis suggested 2. Battery cut from 60 to 22 subtests because too few models beat chance on the rest. Average off-diagonal r=.84 in both datasets.
limits: Dropping subtests where models are at chance removes hard, discriminating items and may inflate g. Spearman vs Pearson mismatch in the write-up.
agent_relevance: A one-factor result depends on which items stay in the battery; our own item set should keep hard items.

source: Krakauer (2026) The Rise and Fall of G in AGI
finding: PCA over 39 models (2019-2025) and 14 benchmarks gives a huge first component that weakens in later model generations.
numbers: PC1 90.0% (5 benchmarks, n=19 raw), 77% detrended; 4-benchmark about 93%, peak 95.5%. Per epoch (4 benchmarks): 79% (n=3), 92% (n=8), 80% (n=7), 64% (n=4). Mean r=.82. Only 246 of 546 cells filled. Residual correlations after PC1: 7 of 10 negative, mean -.24; MATH x GPQA +.59 but GSM8K x GPQA -.80.
limits: Provisional: Epoch IV has n=4 and no degrees of freedom; 42% coverage, non-random gaps; scores from mixed sources; tool-use explanation is a hypothesis; internal inconsistencies (8 vs 6 benchmarks, HumanEval loading .45 vs .20).
agent_relevance: Reasoning-heavy and recall-heavy skills start to separate as models use search or tools. Treat one general level as a snapshot, not a law, when choosing operators per problem class.

source: Burnell, Hao, Conway, Hernandez-Orallo (2023) Revealing the structure of language model capabilities
finding: Using HELM data, three correlated factors (comprehension, language modelling, reasoning) fit better than one general factor.
numbers: 29 LLMs, 27 tasks. Mean task r=.56. 3-factor ML EFA with oblimin: variance .33, .31, .17 (cumulative .82). Fit poor: CFI .70, TLI .61, RMSEA .26. Factor correlations .43 to .51. Log model size r with comprehension .70 [.46,.85], language modelling -.50 [-.72,-.17], reasoning .08 [-.38,.52]. Instruction tuning: positive with reasoning, negative with language modelling; Bayesian EFA agreed.
limits: Tiny sample (29 models); poor fit indices; old models (GPT-3 era); no higher-order test run; instruction tuning effect rests on a few InstructGPT models.
agent_relevance: Size, tuning and recipe move abilities differently, so a scaffold cannot assume bigger model = better at everything. Supports routing by problem class.

source: Anonymous authors (2025) IQ Test for LLMs: An Evaluation Framework
finding: Exploratory factor analysis of 60 LLMs on 44 tasks yields eight latent skills and no reported general factor.
numbers: 60 instruction-tuned models from 24 families; 44 tasks (25 classification, 19 generation). Kaiser plus 85% cumulative variance rule gives 8 factors (General NLU, Token Bias, Document Reading, Truthful Instruction, Domain QA, Social/Ethical, Faithful Summarization, Grad-level Reasoning). Alpha .836, omega .821. Rotation: 26 deg when over-extracting, under 14 deg with 30% of models removed. Arena agreement rho=.73 (13 models).
limits: Models mostly 2-30B open weights; factor labels written by an LLM; the 85% rule forces many factors; only cites Ilic for a general factor. First 100,000 characters of the page read.
agent_relevance: A different battery and method give 8 factors where another gives 1: structure depends on tasks sampled. Caution for any ability-profile claim.

source: Zhou et al. (2026, Nature) General scales unlock AI evaluation with explanatory and predictive power
finding: Replaces benchmark scores with 18-19 human-rated demand dimensions (knowledge, reasoning, metacognition) and predicts per-item success.
numbers: ADeLe battery: 16,108 instances, 20 benchmarks, 15 LLMs. Demand-based random forest: accuracy-weighted AUROC about 0.84 (GPT-4o best, 0.882), calibration error 0.01 versus 0.03 (GloVe) and 0.04 (fine-tuned LLaMA). Demand correlations low to moderate, so dimensions are distinguishable. Many benchmarks fail sensitivity or specificity (non-target demand mean >= 2).
limits: Annotations are by GPT-4o (checked against humans); gains mainly out-of-distribution; battery v1.0 composition decides the correlations.
agent_relevance: A multi-dimensional demand profile predicts item success better than one score. Template for tagging our problem classes by demand level.

source: Hernandez-Orallo et al. (2021) General intelligence disentangled via a generality metric for natural and artificial intelligence
finding: Splits general intelligence into capability and generality; the two can decouple, and diminishing returns in generality are rarely seen.
numbers: Applied to humans, animals, collectives and AI systems on several cognitive and perceptual tests; only the abstract was read, so no further numbers.
limits: Depends on the chosen difficulty function; abstract only.
agent_relevance: Measure whether the agent is broad up to a difficulty level, not only its average score.

source: Ilic and Gignac critic, search-result snippet (2024)
finding: A search snippet says confirmatory factor analysis of 12 benchmarks supports the label achievement rather than intelligence; not opened.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Snippet only; not opened.
agent_relevance: Do not cite numbers from this line.

source: Cucina and Byle (2017) The Bifactor Model Fits Better Than the Higher-Order Model in More Than 90% of Comparisons
finding: Across test batteries the bifactor model of g beats the higher-order model in fit.
numbers: 31 batteries, 58 datasets, 1,712,509 test takers, 166 comparisons. Median gains for bifactor: CFI +.076, TLI +.083, NFI +.078; RMSEA -.028; AIC -1343. Broad factors explain only small variance beyond g in WJ-III, KAIT, KABC, DAS.
limits: Fit advantage can come from unmodelled complexity (Murray and Johnson simulations); Gignac says proportionality violations explain it; parsimony favours higher-order. Fit is not truth.
agent_relevance: Supports framing as one general level plus separate residual skills.

source: Murray and Johnson (2013) bifactor fit bias, as cited in Cucina and Byle (2017)
finding: Monte Carlo work says a bifactor model can win on fit even when a higher-order model is true.
numbers: Second-hand: Morgan, Hodge, Wells and Watkins ran a follow-up simulation; Gignac attributes the fit gap to proportionality violations.
limits: Read only through Cucina and Byle; original not opened.
agent_relevance: Model fit alone cannot settle structure; weigh tests that make different predictions.

source: Johnson et al. and Stankov on g across batteries (via Wikipedia g factor page)
finding: g scores from different batteries on the same people correlate .95 to 1.00, but .79 to .96 when one battery is matrices only.
numbers: Johnson et al. two studies; CFIT lower .79-.96. Stankov: g factors from different batteries are not unity. Kaufman: WJ cognitive g and achievement g highly correlated but not isomorphic.
limits: Secondary (encyclopedia); original papers not opened; years not given.
agent_relevance: g is stable only if the battery is broad; a narrow task set gives a different g.

source: g factor typical numbers (via Wikipedia)
finding: g typically takes 40 to 50% of variance in a human test battery.
numbers: g loadings .10-.90, mean about .60, SD about .15; Raven about .80; Wechsler FSIQ and g scores r>.95. Brain volume with g about .3-.4. Heritability 40-80%, about 50% overall. Non-human animal meta-analysis average cross-ability r=.18.
limits: Encyclopedia summary; the same data fit several rotations, so factor analysis alone does not fix the structure.
agent_relevance: Human g share (about 45%) versus 85-93% in LLM studies: LLM abilities are far more tied together, or batteries are narrower.

source: Spearman (1927); Detterman and Daniel (1989); Tucker-Drob (2009) on SLODR (via Wikipedia)
finding: g explains less when ability is high: tests correlate less among high scorers.
numbers: Spearman 1927: mean r .466 among 12 tests in 78 normal children vs .782 in 22 defective children. Detterman and Daniel: subtest r about .7 (IQ<78) vs about .4 (IQ>122). Tucker-Drob: g about 75% of variance in very low-IQ adults vs 30% in very high-IQ adults.
limits: Secondary source. Deary 1996 and Tucker-Drob criticise splitting by ability group as a test method.
agent_relevance: Strong models may be more specialised, matching the Krakauer drop in PC1 for later epochs.

source: Blum and Holling meta-analysis of SLODR (via Wikipedia)
finding: Meta-analysis supports SLODR for correlations and loadings, which rise with age.
numbers: A sample 2 SD (about 30 IQ points) higher in mean intelligence has an expected mean correlation about .15 lower.
limits: Secondary summary only; unclear whether this means more factorial complexity or an artefact.
agent_relevance: Predicts ability structure changing as agent quality rises.

source: Spearman rivals: sampling theory, mutualism, working memory (via Wikipedia)
finding: Sampling theory and Spearman single-factor model cannot be told apart statistically.
numbers: Critics: forward and backward digit span correlate only modestly while vocabulary and Raven correlate highly; brain damage often gives specific deficits. Working memory-g link is considerably lower in a meta-analysis. Burt: the tetrad law fails for some pairs. Thurstone 13-factor refutation fit g equally after reanalysis.
limits: Encyclopedia level; no original datasets read.
agent_relevance: Do not build the agent on a claim that g is a single mechanism.

source: Carroll (1993) three-stratum theory (via Wikipedia CHC page)
finding: Carroll reanalysed 461 datasets into a three-stratum model: narrow abilities, broad abilities, g.
numbers: About 800 pages. Broad abilities: Gc, Gf, Gq, Grw, Gsm, Glr, Gv, Ga, Gs, plus Gt. Horn (1991) argued 9-10 broad abilities and against g; Carroll held g was essential. Five of seven major intelligence tests are CHC-based.
limits: Critics (Wasserman 2019; Geisinger 2019) doubt the need and empirical basis; cross-battery statistical basis called flawed.
agent_relevance: Use the 9-10 broad ability names as vocabulary to tag problem classes.

source: Wicherts et al. (2004) and Flynn effect gains (via Wikipedia)
finding: Flynn gains are mostly not gains on the latent g factor: factorial invariance across cohorts is not tenable.
numbers: About 2.93 points/decade (Trahan 2014); Pietschnig and Voracek 2015 annual gains .41 fluid, .30 spatial, .28 full-scale, .21 crystallized. WAIS-5 about 1.2 points/decade (Winter 2024). Reversals in Norway and Denmark.
limits: Secondary summary.
agent_relevance: Gains in some abilities do not imply gains in the general level; check what a scaffold really improves.

source: Giangrande et al. (2026) To g or Not to g? Subtest-level Flynn effect ages 7-15
finding: Flynn effect size varies across subtests and is not proportional to g loading.
numbers: N=1187 children, 1957-1999, three WISC versions. Performance IQ gains exceeded full-scale and verbal IQ gains in test-version analyses; cohort analyses showed VIQ>FSIQ>PIQ. Performance subtests gained more than g loadings predict; verbal less.
limits: Mostly White sample (89%); one US longitudinal source.
agent_relevance: The structure of change is not g up; do not assume uniform gains.

source: Austrian Air Force Flynn effect and positive manifold (2025)
finding: A direct test of a weakening positive manifold finds no meaningful change.
numbers: N=204 pilots and air traffic controllers, twelve IQ subtests, 1992-2012. Gains in fluid reasoning, quantitative knowledge, retrieval; working memory and comprehension-knowledge ambiguous. No consistent change in R2 or omega-h (g saturation) across recruitment years.
limits: Small, selected military sample; years with fewer than 10 cases dropped.
agent_relevance: Human g saturation is stable; a falling LLM PC1 reflects model change, not human-like development.

source: Reynolds and Keith, bifactor vs higher-order 'unresolved issue' (via Cucina and Byle 2017)
finding: Higher-order versus bifactor was still called unresolved by Reynolds and Keith.
numbers: Gignac and Murray-Johnson disagree on the cause of bifactor fit advantage.
limits: Narrative reading of a review.
agent_relevance: Treat structure claims as model-dependent.

source: Syed, Lum, Byrne, Skvarc (2024) Examining Working Memory Training for Healthy Adults - A Second-Order Meta-Analysis
finding: Working memory training yields small gains on working memory and little far transfer.
numbers: Six meta-analyses; pooled SMD 0.335 (95% CI .223 to .447, p<.001); no significant difference between training types (adaptive WM, mindfulness, video games, physical activity). Transfer to fluid intelligence and cognitive control minimal. Watrin et al. two-year study: effects only on trained WM tasks.
limits: Healthy adults 18-55; second-order meta-analysis mixes training types.
agent_relevance: Boosting one broad ability by practice does not lift Gf; narrow gains stay narrow.

source: Melby-Lervag, Redick, Hulme (2016) via Syed et al. 2024
finding: Working memory training does not improve far-transfer measures of intelligence (as cited).
numbers: Cited as reporting small near transfer and no reliable far transfer; original not opened.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as above.

source: Wilson et al. (2023) Cross-national generalizability of WISC-V and CHC broad abilities
finding: The five-factor CHC-aligned WISC-V model fits and is strictly invariant across France, Spain and the US.
numbers: Five-factor model excellent fit in each standardization sample; strict factorial invariance supported (change in CFI and TLI within cutoffs). Prior: French vs Swiss WISC-IV only weak invariance (modest Swiss sample).
limits: All Western, nationally representative samples.
agent_relevance: The broad ability labels are stable across languages; usable as problem-class vocabulary.

source: WISC-IV factor structure in low versus normal IQ groups (2026)
finding: In both IQ groups only the bifactor and correlated four-factor models fit; only the correlated four-factor model was invariant.
numbers: Low IQ (<=79) N=141; normal (>80) N=222; 10 WISC-IV subtests; single-factor and higher-order models fit worse. Authors warn FSIQ should be used with caution.
limits: Small samples; SLODR reading only suggested.
agent_relevance: Structure differs by ability band, in line with SLODR; match structure model to the agent strength band.

source: ChatGPT and Bing on a computerized adaptive test of verbal intelligence (2024)
finding: A computerized adaptive vocabulary test puts GPT-3.5 and Bing (GPT-4) above about 95% of humans.
numbers: Three administrations; no difference between models; 42% of repeated items got different answers across sessions; hallucinated answers outside the options; no guessing.
limits: Verbal crystallized ability only; human norms may not transfer; unstable answers.
agent_relevance: Same item gives different answers in different sessions; supports repeat sampling and checks.

source: Krakauer (2026) saturation and ordering effects
finding: Benchmarks saturate, so PC1 changes as the battery changes.
numbers: MMLU asymptote 94%; GPQA Diamond 92%; HumanEval 104% not yet saturated. Leave-one-out: 4-benchmark rotation mean .08 deg; 5-benchmark 1.9 deg (DeepSeek V3 5.58 deg). CUSUM change p=.004.
limits: Ordering by release date conflates trend with structure change.
agent_relevance: A moving structure means any model-ability profile needs refreshing.
